newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain to cut debt/GDP ratio, ending 9-year growth.
newsitem.headline: Spain to cut debt/GDP ratio, ending 9-year growth.

text.p: In an effort to help launch Europe's single currency, Spain may finally put an end to nine years of growth in its debt to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio, analysts said.
Despite a tame deficit, Spain's 1996 debt/GDP ratio grew by more than three full points to around 69 percent from 66 percent a year earlier to continue an uptrend dating from 1988.

But analysts did not expect that trend to continue and keep the government from meeting its target this year and bringing the ratio back to around 67 percent in December, despite an expected deficit of two trillion pesetas ($13.8 billion).

"With a deficit to gross domestic product at three percent and nominal growth at around 5.6 percent, by definition, they will bring down debt to gross domestic product," said Luca Jellinek, economist at Paribas Capital market in London.

Even apart from the government's forecast for three-percent GDP growth and 2.6 percent inflation, a fall in the debt to GDP ratio is possible because the government could use privatisation proceeds and money the Treasury has deposited at the Bank of Spain to help cover the two trillion deficit.
Societe Generale in Madrid expected debt to GDP to fall to 66.5 percent, while Salomon Brothers in London forecasts it to drop to around 66.7 percent.

And some analysts said Spain's primary deficit, or the deficit without financial expenditures, should be positive in 1997 for the first time ever. "They were almost there in 1996, and they should make it this year," said Carmen Alcaide, analyst at BBV here.
In February, as the Spanish Treasury cashed in around 608 billion pesetas from selling its 20.9 percent of Telefonica, it said it would use 375 billion of the pesetas to cut its level of debt.

And more privatisations are expected. The government has already said it will sell its remaining 10-percent Repsol stake in April or May, while another part of Endesa is expected to go public in October.
The government is also considering using part of its deep current account with the Bank of Spain to fund part of the 1996 deficit.
At the end of 1995, the Spanish Treasury had 2.53 trillion pesetas versus 1.56 trillion at the end of 1996 in its account.
Although the Maastricht Treaty targets the debt to GDP ratio below 60 percent, it seems more crucial that of the goal can not be met that the ratio at least shows a falling trend toward that level.

"Government moves to cut the debt ratio significantly this year should buttress Spain's bargaining position prior to the spring 1998 selection of EMU (economic and monetary union) founding members," Salomon said in a note to clients.
Spain's central government domestic debt level was 36 trillion pesetas at the end of 1996. This rose to 43.8 trillion pesetas if loans and foreign debt are taken into account.
And at the end of September 1996, Spanish local and regional governments also had 7.42 billion pesetas in debt.
Spain's 1996 GDP stands at 73.661 trillion pesetas.
-- Tiziana Barghini, Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340 ($ = 145.0 Spanish Pesetas)
